title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 97–98
description: Advanced vocabulary for context-appropriate registers, spoken and written style, and British–American usage contrasts, with original examples and Brazilian Portuguese translations.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study based on the user-provided edition. Targets and usage contrasts follow the study pages, exercises and answer key; examples and notes are original and do not reproduce textbook passages, exercises or illustrations.

audit.scope: Teaching pages for Units 97 and 98, including vocabulary tables, registers, usage notes and UK–US contrasts; exercises 97.1–97.5 and 98.1–98.3; related answer-key explanations.
audit.pronunciation: British English is the broad IPA baseline, supplied only for confidently transcribed short items. Empty IPA for most longer expressions avoids speculative connected-speech transcriptions and should not imply silence.
audit.languagePolicy: English for all fields except pt, which contains natural Brazilian Portuguese translations.
audit.reviewMethod: Reviewed the two complete teaching units, exercises and matching answer key. Curated core register terms, relevant exercise-only contrasts and UK–US equivalents. Independently authored examples and notes; checked original versus exercise-only provenance, JSON schema parity, unique IDs, field types and static audio-target constraints.
audit.limitations: No MP3 audio is bundled, and browser import, text-to-speech pronunciation and speech recognition were not tested. Regional conventions and formal titles vary by setting; the cards describe the source book’s contrasts without claiming strict geographic exclusivity.

units.title: Unit 97 — Register: degrees of formality
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 97. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Language style · formality, spoken and written register, historical usage
learningObjectives: Distinguish neutral, formal and informal choices without assuming one is universally preferable.
Identify expressions mainly associated with everyday speech or with formal written discourse.
Recognise outdated, archaic, literary, academic and technical language and choose context-appropriate alternatives.
Use contrasts from the exercises, including British informal terms, formal synonyms and register-specific discourse markers.

sectionsChecked: A · Formal and informal words and register guidance

items.pt: registro de linguagem; grau de formalidade
items.example: The editor adjusted the register of the letter to suit its intended audience.
items.note: Register involves tone and the relationship between speaker and listener or writer and reader.

items.example: Her partner joined the group for dinner after the conference.
items.note: Neutral term for a romantic partner, regardless of marital status.

items.example: Marcus is travelling with his other half this weekend.
items.note: An informal, affectionate way to refer to a spouse or partner.

items.example: The bloke at reception found my missing umbrella.
items.note: Very common informal British English for a man; avoid in formal reports.

items.example: The guy who repaired the projector was very helpful.
items.note: Informal word for a man; also occurs more broadly in American English.

items.example: The visiting researchers conversed with local engineers after the lecture.
items.note: More formal than talk or chat; converse with someone.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: The documentary was broadcast on national television.
items.note: Neutral term; TV is a standard abbreviation.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: We watched the rugby on the telly after supper.
items.note: Informal, especially British English; unlike formal television.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: My grandfather still calls the television the box.
items.note: An informal, somewhat old-fashioned nickname for television.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: She put on her glasses to read the timetable.
items.note: Neutral everyday term for spectacles.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: His spectacles slipped down his nose as he read the document.
items.note: A more formal or traditional word for glasses.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: Have you seen my specs anywhere near the sofa?
items.note: Informal shortened form of spectacles.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: Please bring warm clothes for the mountain excursion.
items.note: Neutral term for what people wear.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: Protective clothing is required in the laboratory.
items.note: More formal or general than clothes; normally uncountable.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: The exhibition displays garments made from recycled fibres.
items.note: Often refers to individual items of clothing in retail or formal descriptions.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: They packed their camping gear before sunrise.
items.note: Informal collective word; the intended sense varies with context and can include equipment.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: We use this method to check the integrity of the data.
items.note: Neutral alternative to employ and utilise.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: The researchers employed a different sampling method.
items.note: A more formal synonym for use in this sense; also means hire workers.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: The system utilises spare memory to reduce processing delays.
items.note: A relatively formal alternative to use; not automatically preferable in clear writing.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: I'll try to finish the report before Friday.
items.note: Neutral alternative to attempt and endeavour.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: The team attempted to recover the corrupted archive.
items.note: More formal than try; common in technical and official writing.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: The organisation will endeavour to answer enquiries within two days.
items.note: Formal British spelling; often followed by to + infinitive.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: Would you like to have a go at solving this puzzle?
items.note: Informal British expression for making an attempt; can also mean criticise in another context.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: I'll have a stab at the answer even though I'm not completely sure.
items.note: Informal expression suggesting an uncertain attempt.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: She had a bash at assembling the furniture herself.
items.note: Informal, mainly British; describes trying something.

items.pt: tentar; dar uma chance a si mesmo (informal)
items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: We decided to have a crack at the hardest exercise first.
items.note: Informal expression for attempting something challenging.

items.section: A · Formal, neutral and informal equivalents
items.example: He had a shot at the scholarship and was shortlisted.
items.note: Informal expression for making an attempt; commonly followed by at.

items.example: The initial trial failed; subsequently, the researchers redesigned the experiment.
items.note: Mainly written linking adverb; later or afterwards is commoner in speech.

items.example: In sum, the evidence supports a more cautious conclusion.
items.note: Formal written expression that summarises an argument.

items.example: I spoke to whatsisname from the finance department yesterday.
items.note: Very informal spoken substitute when a man's name cannot be recalled.

items.example: Whatsername from the workshop called again this morning.
items.note: Very informal spoken substitute when a woman's name cannot be recalled.

items.example: Pass me that little thingy for opening the battery compartment.
items.note: Informal spoken placeholder when the object's name is forgotten.

items.pt: mas veja bem; por outro lado; ainda assim
items.example: The hotel was expensive. Mind you, breakfast was excellent.
items.note: Spoken discourse marker qualifying or contrasting a previous point.

items.example: Now then, does everyone understand the emergency procedure?
items.note: Typically spoken phrase used to gain attention or open a new part of a conversation.

items.example: The poem contains archaic expressions that require explanatory notes.
items.note: A word or usage belonging to an earlier stage of the language; not simply formal.

items.example: His greeting sounded old-fashioned but perfectly polite.
items.note: Used of expressions no longer typical in modern conversation.

items.pt: antigo termo para hospital psiquiátrico; asilo
items.example: The historical article described conditions in a nineteenth-century asylum.
items.note: Historically used for a psychiatric hospital; outdated and potentially stigmatising in this sense.

items.example: The novel describes a child wearing a freshly pressed frock.
items.note: Old-fashioned term for a dress in many British contexts.

items.example: The elderly character listened to the news on the wireless.
items.note: An older British term for a radio; nowadays often refers to wireless technology instead.

items.example: The historian noted that consumption appeared in many nineteenth-century medical records.
items.note: Historic term for tuberculosis, not the modern sense of using goods or resources.

items.example: The antique portrait shows a man holding a pair of eyeglasses.
items.note: The book treats this as old-fashioned; the term is still current in some varieties of English, notably US English.

items.example: The legal document refers to the owner's offspring rather than children.
items.note: Formal or technical alternative to children; its singular and plural forms are identical.

items.example: The kids spent the whole afternoon playing in the garden.
items.note: Informal alternative to children.

items.example: I always carry sunglasses when driving in bright sunlight.
items.note: Neutral term; shades is informal.

items.example: He put on his shades before leaving the café.
items.note: Informal word for sunglasses, particularly common in speech.

items.example: A police officer helped the visitors find their way.
items.note: Neutral, gender-inclusive occupational term.

items.example: A cop directed traffic away from the accident.
items.note: Informal term for a police officer; not appropriate in many official contexts.

items.example: The detective novel refers to a bobby patrolling the street.
items.note: Informal, traditional British word for a police officer; less common today.

items.example: I left my umbrella in the office yesterday.
items.note: Neutral term, contrasted with informal British brolly.

items.example: Take a brolly; those clouds look threatening.
items.note: Informal British word for umbrella.

items.example: Her feedback was invaluable during the final revision.
items.note: More emphatic and formal than really useful; it does not mean without value.

items.example: That checklist was really useful during the installation.
items.note: Conversational alternative to invaluable in many contexts, though not equally emphatic.

items.example: Please ensure that every participant has received the updated schedule.
items.note: Formal alternative to make sure in instructions and documents.

items.example: Make sure the laptop is switched off before packing it.
items.note: Neutral, conversational alternative to ensure.

items.example: The report frequently refers to earlier research on the topic.
items.note: Often associated with written language relative to often in speech.

items.example: Let's start as soon as everyone arrives.
items.note: In the book's corpus comparison, more characteristic of speech than begin.

items.example: The ceremony will begin shortly after midday.
items.note: More frequent in written material than start in the book's corpus comparison; both are normal.

items.example: Maybe we could postpone the call until tomorrow.
items.note: Particularly common in everyday speech; perhaps may sound more neutral or formal.

items.example: The evidence was incomplete; moreover, the sample was unusually small.
items.note: Written connective adding a further supporting argument.

items.section: Exercises · Archaic, literary and technical register
items.example: The historical drama features an apothecary preparing herbal remedies.
items.note: Old-fashioned term for a person who prepared and sold medicines.

items.section: Exercises · Archaic, literary and technical register
items.example: The medieval tale describes a damsel awaiting rescue.
items.note: Archaic or literary term for a young woman; may sound patronising today.

items.section: Exercises · Archaic, literary and technical register
items.example: Her dissertation examines the meaning of poesy in early modern literature.
items.note: Archaic or literary alternative to poetry.

items.section: Exercises · Archaic, literary and technical register
items.example: The play uses whither where modern speakers would usually say where to.
items.note: Archaic adverb of direction; not used in normal contemporary conversation.

items.section: Exercises · Archaic, literary and technical register
items.example: The researchers challenged the prevailing paradigm in the field.
items.note: Academic term for an established framework of theories or methods.

items.pt: aquisição de segunda língua (sigla em inglês)
items.section: Exercises · Archaic, literary and technical register
items.example: The article reviews competing approaches to SLA.
items.note: Academic abbreviation for second language acquisition; in speech normally pronounced as separate letters.

items.section: Exercises · Archaic, literary and technical register
items.example: The playwright deliberately used thee to evoke older English.
items.note: Archaic object form of singular you, found especially in older poetry and religious texts.

items.pt: é; isto é (forma arcaica de it is)
items.section: Exercises · Archaic, literary and technical register
items.example: The character says ’tis in an imitation of an old play.
items.note: Archaic contraction of it is, mainly encountered in literature.

items.section: Exercises · Archaic, literary and technical register
items.example: Her apparently harsh comment was meant in jest.
items.note: Literary or formal expression meaning as a joke.

items.section: Exercises · Archaic, literary and technical register
items.example: A sense of weariness spread through the team after the long journey.
items.note: Literary or formal noun for fatigue or tiredness.

items.section: Exercises · Archaic, literary and technical register
items.example: He responded with feigned surprise when his friends arrived.
items.note: Literary/formal adjective meaning pretended or not genuine.

items.section: Exercises · Archaic, literary and technical register
items.example: She left early cos she had a train to catch.
items.note: Informal written representation of a spoken reduction; avoid in standard formal writing.

items.section: Exercises · Archaic, literary and technical register
items.example: Yeah, I remember the meeting you're talking about.
items.note: Very common informal conversational equivalent of yes.

units.title: Unit 98 — Divided by a common language
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 98. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Varieties of English · British and American vocabulary
learningObjectives: Compare British and American everyday terms for roads, travel directions and public facilities.
Understand differences in university, school, academic-year and academic-title terminology.
Recognise corresponding household and electrical terms across the two varieties.
Interpret regional language as a usage preference rather than a blanket rule about correctness.

sectionsChecked: A · Streets and roads and Language help

items.pt: atravessar a rua (mais comum em inglês americano)
items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: Use the crossing lights before you cross the street.
items.note: Street is widely used in American English where British English often prefers road.

items.pt: atravessar a rua (mais comum em inglês britânico)
items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: Please cross the road at the marked crossing.
items.note: A common British choice, especially when talking about a busy road.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: The restaurant is two blocks away from the station.
items.note: US use in directions for the distance between intersecting streets.

items.pt: locadora de carros; aluguel de automóveis
items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: The car rental desk is next to the airport information point.
items.note: Common US expression; British English often uses car hire.

items.pt: na diagonal; do lado diagonalmente oposto (EUA informal)
items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: The pharmacy is kitty-corner to the supermarket.
items.note: Informal US expression for diagonally opposite; also written catty-corner.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: The café is diagonally opposite the post office.
items.note: British/international equivalent of American kitty-corner.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: We stopped at a gas station before joining the highway.
items.note: Typical US term for a place selling fuel; British equivalent is petrol station.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: There is a petrol station just beyond the roundabout.
items.note: Typical British equivalent of US gas station.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: The driver stopped to let pedestrians cross at the crosswalk.
items.note: US term; British equivalents include pedestrian crossing and zebra crossing.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: A pedestrian crossing has been added outside the school.
items.note: General British term for a marked place to cross the road.

items.pt: faixa de pedestres tipo zebra (inglês britânico)
items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: She waited beside the zebra crossing for the cars to stop.
items.note: A particular kind of pedestrian crossing with contrasting stripes in British English.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: The trail follows the river through the woods.
items.note: Often US usage for a path in the countryside.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: A narrow path leads from the cottage to the lake.
items.note: Common British equivalent in the walking context of US trail.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: A small creek runs behind the farmhouse.
items.note: In this context a small river or stream; creek may have other regional meanings.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: We crossed the stream using the wooden footbridge.
items.note: Common British equivalent of US creek in the book's example.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: Take a left at the next traffic lights.
items.note: US conversational direction equivalent to turn left.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: Turn left just after the museum.
items.note: Neutral/British equivalent of American take a left.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: We joined the Interstate after leaving the city.
items.note: US term for a major motorway in the Interstate Highway System; usually capitalised in the named system.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: The motorway was closed following a serious accident.
items.note: British equivalent in broad road-category terms, not an exact administrative match for every US Interstate.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: Traffic was backed up near the intersection.
items.note: US road term; British English usually prefers junction in this context.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: Turn right at the junction with the main road.
items.note: Common British equivalent of intersection.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: A shopping cart was blocking one of the parking spaces.
items.note: US equivalent of British shopping trolley.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: He returned the shopping trolley after unloading the bags.
items.note: British equivalent of US shopping cart.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: The parking lot fills up before eight on weekdays.
items.note: US term for a car park.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: The museum has a free car park for visitors.
items.note: British term for a parking lot.

items.pt: dar ré; recuar com o veículo (inglês americano)
items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: The driver had to back up to make room for the van.
items.note: US term in this driving context; also has many other meanings.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: Could you reverse a little so I can get past?
items.note: A standard British alternative to back up when driving backwards.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: The exit is immediately after the overpass.
items.note: US term for a road bridge over another road; flyover in British usage.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: They built a flyover to reduce congestion at the junction.
items.note: British counterpart of US overpass in road contexts.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: Their office is located downtown near the courthouse.
items.note: Common US adverb/adjective for a city's central commercial area.

items.section: A · Streets and roads, US and UK
items.example: The new tram line runs through the city centre.
items.note: British equivalent in this context of US downtown.

items.pt: cursar faculdade; ir para a universidade (uso americano)
items.example: She hopes to go to college after graduating from high school.
items.note: In US English college often refers broadly to higher education; UK college commonly has other meanings.

items.pt: instituição de ensino pós-16 anos; faculdade (dependendo do país)
items.example: The British student enrolled at a local college to study engineering skills.
items.note: UK college can be an institution for further or specialist education, not necessarily a university.

items.example: He went to university in Edinburgh to study physics.
items.note: In Britain go to university is the usual broad expression for higher education.

items.pt: matéria; disciplina cursada (uso americano, neste contexto)
items.example: She is taking three courses this semester.
items.note: In the book's US context course can mean an individual subject or class; UK speakers often say module.

items.example: This module covers mathematical methods for engineering.
items.note: Typical UK term for a component of a degree programme.

items.example: The new semester begins in late September.
items.note: Used in both varieties, though UK institutions may also organise teaching in terms.

items.pt: período letivo; trimestre ou etapa do ano acadêmico
items.example: The next term starts after the winter break.
items.note: Common British label for an academic period; structure varies across institutions.

items.example: As a freshman, she joined the university debating society.
items.note: US term for a first-year student; language may vary by institution.

items.example: The fresher signed up for several clubs during induction week.
items.note: Informal British word for a student in the first year of university.

items.example: By her sophomore year, she had decided on her main subject.
items.note: US label for a student in the second year of a four-year programme.

items.example: He's a second year studying computer science.
items.note: British way of referring to a student in year two; also second-year student.

items.example: As a junior, he completed an internship at a design firm.
items.note: US label for a third-year student, particularly in four-year programmes.

items.example: The third years are preparing their final-year projects.
items.note: UK equivalent in the book's comparison with US juniors.

items.pt: ter como área principal de graduação (EUA)
items.example: She decided to major in chemistry after her first year.
items.note: US academic expression; major in + subject.

items.pt: fazer graduação com especialização ou honras em (uso britânico)
items.example: He chose to do honours in French at university.
items.note: The book's UK expression for studying a principal subject; exact honours-degree systems vary.

items.example: She graduated with an honours degree in history.
items.note: A degree classification or qualification, not a literal prize; rules vary by institution.

items.pt: professor universitário; docente com título de professor
items.example: The professor was available to discuss the students' proposals.
items.note: In the US often a broad form of address for university teachers; in the UK professor generally denotes a senior academic rank.

items.example: The lecturer explained the assignment requirements at the end of class.
items.note: In Britain lecturer is a common term for a university teacher; titles and career structures vary.

items.example: He works at an elementary school in Oregon.
items.note: US counterpart, at broadly similar ages, of British primary school.

items.pt: escola primária; anos iniciais do ensino fundamental (Reino Unido)
items.example: Her daughter starts primary school this autumn.
items.note: British counterpart of US elementary school.

items.example: They met when they were both in high school.
items.note: US expression for secondary education, though grades and institution arrangements vary.

items.pt: escola secundária; ensino médio e anos finais (Reino Unido)
items.example: She has taught science at a secondary school for a decade.
items.note: British equivalent at a broad level to US high school; exact age ranges differ.

items.example: The electrician checked that the appliance had a safe ground connection.
items.note: US electrical term, equivalent to British earth in this sense; also has unrelated meanings.

items.example: The technician connected the earth wire to the correct terminal.
items.note: British electrical term, equivalent to US ground in this context.

items.pt: caçamba de lixo; contêiner de resíduos (EUA)
items.example: A dumpster was placed outside the building during renovation.
items.note: US word for a large rubbish container; UK equivalent is skip in the book.

items.pt: caçamba de entulho ou lixo (Reino Unido)
items.example: We hired a skip for the broken furniture and building waste.
items.note: British word for a large container used for rubbish or renovation waste.

items.example: The bathroom faucet has started leaking again.
items.note: US equivalent of British tap.

items.example: Turn off the tap before you leave the kitchen.
items.note: British equivalent of US faucet in this household sense.

items.example: The apartment has a new stove with an electric oven.
items.note: In the book, US equivalent of British cooker; stove has a wider range of senses.

items.example: They replaced the old cooker when they renovated the kitchen.
items.note: British everyday word for a large appliance used for cooking.

items.example: Heat the oil in a skillet before adding the vegetables.
items.note: US equivalent of British frying pan; often a fairly deep pan.

items.example: She cooked the omelette in a non-stick frying pan.
items.note: Standard British equivalent of American skillet.
